content: The study conducted in Western Kenya, identified as Trial ID ISRCTN30012997 (2012), focused on evaluating health outcomes among infants. Another trial, ISRCTN10309022 (2018), assessed the effectiveness of a legume-enriched nutritional intervention for treating severe undernutrition in children. Research by Iuel-Brockdorf et al. (2015) in Burkina Faso examined the acceptability of new formulations of corn-soy blends and lipid-based nutrient supplements. A subsequent study in 2016 by the same group evaluated the acceptability of improved supplementary foods for treating moderate acute malnutrition using a mixed-method approach. Jaeggi et al. (2015) found that iron fortification negatively impacted the gut microbiome, increased pathogen abundance, and induced intestinal inflammation in Kenyan infants. Jahari et al. (2000) demonstrated that energy and micronutrient supplementation improved skeletal maturation in undernourished Indonesian children. Jalla et al. (2002) investigated zinc absorption and exchangeable zinc pool sizes in breastfed infants fed meat or cereal as their first complementary food. Javan et al. (2017) conducted a randomized clinical trial in Iran, showing the effectiveness of supplementary blended flour based on chickpea and cereals for treating moderate acute malnutrition in infants. Javid et al. (1991) explored the interactions between infections, malnutrition, and iron nutritional status in Pakistani infants through a longitudinal study. Jilcott et al. (2010) designed, implemented, and evaluated a supplemental feeding program for underweight children aged 6–59 months in Western Uganda. John and Gopaldas (1993) evaluated the impact of a controlled 6-month feeding trial on the growth of children aged 6–24 months, comparing high-energy, low-bulk gruel to high-energy, high-bulk gruel. Jong-Mee Lee and Hea-Jin Park (2005) studied the effects of a supplementary diet on iron status and development in infants. Kaimila et al. (2019) reported the development of acute malnutrition despite nutritional supplementation in Malawi. Kajjura et al. (2019) assessed the effect of a novel supplementary porridge on the nutritional status of infants and young children with moderate acute malnutrition in Uganda through a cluster-randomized controlled trial. Kalavi et al. (1996) examined the effects of tempe-yellow maize porridge and milk-yellow maize porridge on growth rate, diarrhea, and rehabilitation duration in malnourished children. Kalhoff et al. (2020) investigated the effects of LC-PUFA supply via complementary food on infant development in a randomized controlled trial. Kampstra et al. (2018) demonstrated that adding amylase to fortified blended foods increased energy and nutrient intake by 47–67% among Burkinabe children aged 12–35 months. Karakochuk et al. (2012) found that ready-to-use supplementary food resulted in higher recovery rates compared to corn-soy blend in treating moderate acute malnutrition in Ethiopian children. Kekalih et al. (2019) outlined a multicenter randomized controlled trial protocol for food supplement intervention for wasting children in Indonesia. King et al. (2007) studied the impact of high-diastase malted barley flour on the weight and height of malnourished children in Panama. Kodkany et al. (2013) demonstrated that biofortification of pearl millet with iron and zinc increased mineral absorption above physiological requirements in young children. Konyole et al. (2013) assessed the acceptability of complementary foods with indigenous animal-source foods and corn-soy blend plus among Kenyan children and mothers. Konyole et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of improved animal-source foods and micronutrient-fortified complementary foods on lean mass, linear growth, and iron status in Kenyan children. Krebs et al. (2006) explored the feasibility and impact of meat as a first complementary food for breastfed infants on zinc intake and status. Krebs et al. (2012) compared complementary feeding strategies to meet zinc requirements in older breastfed infants. Kuusipalo et al. (2006) investigated growth and changes in blood hemoglobin concentration among underweight Malawian infants receiving fortified spreads for 12 weeks. Lachat et al. (2006) found that processing complementary food did not increase hair zinc levels or growth in infants in rural Tanzania. LaGrone et al. (2012) demonstrated that a novel fortified blended flour was not inferior to lipid-based ready-to-use supplementary foods for treating moderate acute malnutrition in Malawian children. Langendorf et al. (2014) conducted a prospective intervention study in Niger to prevent acute malnutrition among young children in crises. Leroy et al. (2020) reported that a food-assisted maternal and child health and nutrition program in Burundi increased household food security, energy, and micronutrient consumption, as well as maternal and child dietary diversity. Macharia-Mutie et al. (2012) showed that maize porridge enriched with a micronutrient powder containing low-dose iron reduced anemia and iron deficiency in Kenyan preschool children. Manary et al. (2004) demonstrated the effectiveness of home-based therapy for severe malnutrition using ready-to-use food. Mallard et al. (2014) found that dietary diversity at six months of age was associated with subsequent growth and mediated the effect of maternal education on infant growth in urban Zambia.
